content: Mixed-handedness, also referred to as cross-dominance or mixed laterality, is a phenomenon in which an individual demonstrates a preference for using one hand for certain fine motor tasks while favoring the other hand for different tasks. This is distinct from true ambidexterity, where both hands are equally skilled. For example, some police officers may hold a firearm with one hand but write with the other. Mixed laterality can also extend to preferences involving other body parts, such as eyes, ears, or feet, on opposite sides of the body. Cross-dominance can present challenges in activities requiring precise aim, such as shooting. Ambidexterity is a well-known form of cross-dominance, characterized by equal proficiency in using both hands (or, to a lesser extent, feet). The term ambidextrous originates from the Latin words ambi, meaning both, and dexter, meaning right or favorable, literally translating to right on both sides. While ambidexterity is rare at birth, it can be developed through practice. The process involves performing simple daily tasks, such as brushing teeth or opening doors, with the non-dominant hand. Over time, these tasks become easier. More complex skills, like writing or throwing with both hands, require significant patience and practice but are achievable. Even among ambidextrous individuals, there is often a tendency to favor one hand for specific tasks. The degree of skill with each hand determines the extent of ambidexterity. This phenomenon is linked to the brain's control over the opposite side of the body, and some individuals may experience hesitation when deciding which side to use for a particular task. In modern times, ambidexterity is more commonly observed in individuals who were originally left-handed but adapted to using their right hand, often due to societal or institutional pressures, such as schools emphasizing right-handed habits. Additionally, many everyday tools and devices are designed for right-handed users, forcing left-handed individuals to develop motor skills in their non-dominant hand. For example, left-handed people may need to use a can opener with their right hand. Consequently, left-handed individuals are more likely to develop ambidextrous skills compared to right-handed individuals, who are not typically exposed to left-favoring tools. Ambidexterity is often encouraged in activities requiring high levels of skill with both hands, such as juggling, swimming, playing percussion or keyboard instruments, performing surgery, and engaging in combat. In sports, ambidexterity offers significant advantages. In baseball, for instance, switch hitting allows a batter to choose the side of the plate that provides the greatest advantage against a pitcher of the opposite hand. Pete Rose, the all-time hits leader in Major League Baseball, was a switch hitter. Similarly, Tony Mullane, a 19th-century pitcher with 284 career wins, was ambidextrous. In soccer, ambidexterity enables players to shoot effectively from either side, making it difficult for defenders to predict or block their shots. Goalkeepers also benefit from being equally adept at diving to either side. In sports like pool and snooker, ambidexterity allows players to reach shots more easily by switching hands, as demonstrated by two-time snooker world champion Ronnie O'Sullivan. Other sports where cross-dominance is advantageous include basketball, where players may pass or shoot with their weaker hand; hockey and ice hockey, where players can shoot from either side; and combat sports, where fighters can adopt either a right-handed or left-handed stance. In skateboarding, the ability to skate proficiently with both feet, known as switch skating, is highly beneficial, as is the case in surfing, where ambidextrous surfers are referred to as switch-foot. In golf, left-handed players using right-handed clubs may achieve better control and stronger drives due to enhanced coordination in their left hand. In tennis, ambidexterity allows players to reach backhand shots more effectively with their weaker hand. Notable ambidextrous tennis players include Maria Sharapova and Luke Jensen. The term ambidexter originally had a legal connotation in English, referring to jurors who accepted bribes from both parties involved in a case. Such jurors, if found guilty, were required to forfeit decies tantum, an amount ten times the value of the bribes they received.
